domain-item:d078-conversation-analysis.label: Conversation analysis (CA) of talk-in-interaction

requirement_scope.rationale: Study how participants organize naturally occurring interaction turn by turn, including turn-taking, sequence organization, repair and the actions accomplished through talk. Use recordings and sufficiently detailed transcripts, analyze cases closely, and ground claims in participants’ displayed orientations. CA is distinct from CDA and generic thematic coding.

domain-item:d078-conversation-analysis.requirement_reason: Optional. This belongs to the method you selected. You can continue without choosing it.
domain-item:d078-conversation-analysis.meaning: Conversation analysis studies how people organise talk, turn by turn, in a recording of real interaction. The evidence is the sequence: who speaks, how the next turn responds, and how repair happens. Claims should be grounded in what the participants treat as relevant. It is not the same as critical discourse analysis or a general theme code.
domain-item:d078-conversation-analysis.learner_output: An analysis tied to the transcript, with the sequential evidence and the transcription conventions. Automatic speech or text measures may help you find passages. They do not replace the sequential reading.

domain-item:d078-count-regression.label: Count regression: Poisson and negative binomial models

requirement_scope.rationale: Model non-negative event counts with exposure/offset and dependence structure represented appropriately. Start with Poisson when its mean-variance structure is plausible; consider negative binomial when overdispersion is supported, and diagnose zero inflation, clustering and excess zeros rather than selecting by habit.

domain-item:d078-count-regression.requirement_reason: Optional. This belongs to the method you selected. You can continue without choosing it.
domain-item:d078-count-regression.meaning: Poisson and negative binomial models are for counts of events. Include the exposure, such as time or population at risk, when the design has one. Start with Poisson when its assumptions fit. Use the negative binomial when the counts vary more than Poisson expects. Check extra zeros and clustering rather than choosing a model by habit.
domain-item:d078-count-regression.learner_output: The model, the exposure, the dispersion checks, predicted rates or effects, and the uncertainty. The model does not create a causal result.

domain-item:experiments-quasi-experiment.label: Experiments, quasi-experiments and causal inference

requirement_scope.rationale: Use when the question asks about causal effects and the design can support a defensible comparison with explicit assumptions.

domain-item:experiments-quasi-experiment.requirement_reason: An optional focus for a narrower question. You can continue through Social Sciences without it. Select it when that work fits what you want to learn.
domain-item:experiments-quasi-experiment.learner_output: A design note naming the treatment/exposure, comparison, outcome, timing, identification assumptions, threats to validity and limits of the causal claim.

relationships.note: Causal claims require explicit checks of design validity and uncertainty.
Evaluation may use causal designs when the intervention and assumptions support them.

limitations: Randomisation or a quasi-experimental label does not automatically make a causal claim credible; assumptions and implementation must be examined.
Results may be specific to the population, intervention and setting studied.
domain-item:experiments-quasi-experiment.meaning: Design comparisons that help estimate whether an intervention or exposure contributed to an outcome, while making the assumptions and possible confounding visible.

learning_links.locator: Open textbook chapters on potential outcomes, experiments, matching, instrumental variables and quasi-experimental designs
learning_links.scope_note: A broad causal-inference text; select chapters appropriate to the design and do not treat an estimator as a substitute for identification reasoning.

learning_links.scope_note: Worked examples support learning; they do not determine whether a learner's own design identifies a causal effect.

domain-item:focus-groups-and-workshops.label: Focus groups and workshops

requirement_scope.condition: Study how people discuss a topic together and how group interaction shapes evidence.
requirement_scope.rationale: Use when the question benefits from group discussion or interaction; group dynamics are part of the evidence and may not suit sensitive topics or questions requiring private individual accounts.

domain-item:focus-groups-and-workshops.requirement_reason: A useful option for the work described above. It is not required for every Social Sciences student. You can continue without it and come back if you need it.
domain-item:focus-groups-and-workshops.learner_output: A moderator guide, ethically managed session record and analysis showing both what participants said and how group interaction shaped the evidence.

relationships.note: The question determines whether interaction between participants is part of the evidence.
Transcripts or notes still need a documented analytic approach.

limitations: Group discussion can be shaped by dominant voices, silence, conformity, privacy limits and the group composition.
Findings from a purposive group do not automatically represent a wider population or establish causality.
domain-item:focus-groups-and-workshops.meaning: Use a guided group discussion to learn how people explain, agree, disagree and build on one another's views.

domain-item:longitudinal-panel-and-multi.label: Longitudinal, panel and multilevel data

requirement_scope.rationale: Use when observations repeat over time or are nested in groups; the data structure changes the analysis and assumptions.

domain-item:longitudinal-panel-and-multi.requirement_reason: An optional focus for a narrower question. You can continue through Social Sciences without it. Select it when that work fits what you want to learn.
domain-item:longitudinal-panel-and-multi.learner_output: A data-structure and analysis plan identifying units, time points, levels, missingness, model assumptions and the limits of the conclusions.

relationships.note: Model choice and interpretation require explicit assumptions and uncertainty checks.
R is one possible implementation environment, not a requirement of the design.

limitations: A sophisticated model cannot repair poor measurement, missing data or an unsuitable research design.
Repeated observations and clustered data require assumptions that should be explained rather than hidden behind software output.
domain-item:longitudinal-panel-and-multi.meaning: Analyse data collected repeatedly over time or collected in groups within groups, while accounting for the dependence and structure those designs create.

domain-item:measurement-and-operationali.label: Turning ideas into observable measures

requirement_scope.rationale: Turning an abstract construct into observable indicators is valuable when a project measures concepts, especially structured quantitative or instrument-based work, but is not required in the same form by every interpretive or non-empirical route.

domain-item:measurement-and-operationali.requirement_reason: A useful option for the work described above. It is not required for every Social Sciences student. You can continue without it and come back if you need it.
domain-item:measurement-and-operationali.learner_output: A small measurement plan showing the concept, indicators, questions or observations, and their limitations.

relationships.note: A clear question helps determine what needs to be measured.

limitations: A measure is an indicator of an idea, not the idea itself.
Different groups may understand or answer the same measure differently.
domain-item:measurement-and-operationali.meaning: Turn an idea such as trust, wellbeing or access into questions, observations or records that can be examined, while explaining what the measure leaves out.

learning_links.label: Learn how concepts become measurable indicators

domain-item:open-science-preregistration.label: Keeping a clear, repeatable research record

requirement_scope.rationale: Transparent records and reproducible materials can strengthen inspectability; preregistration is not suitable or possible for every study and sharing may be restricted.

domain-item:open-science-preregistration.requirement_reason: A useful option for the work described above. It is not required for every Social Sciences student. You can continue without it and come back if you need it.
domain-item:open-science-preregistration.learner_output: An organised research record with a plan, data dictionary or codebook, versioned materials and a note explaining deviations.

relationships.note: A traceable research record also needs organised sources and materials.

limitations: What can be shared depends on consent, privacy, security, copyright and other rules.
Reproducibility does not make an unsuitable research design valid.
domain-item:open-science-preregistration.meaning: Record plans, decisions, data descriptions, code, materials and changes so another person can inspect how the work was done and, where possible, repeat it.

domain-item:participatory-and-action-res.label: Participatory and action research

requirement_scope.condition: Involve affected communities in framing questions, design, interpretation or action.
requirement_scope.rationale: Use when affected people should help shape the question, design, interpretation or action; participation and power-sharing are central.

domain-item:participatory-and-action-res.requirement_reason: A useful option for the work described above. It is not required for every Social Sciences student. You can continue without it and come back if you need it.
domain-item:participatory-and-action-res.learner_output: A participation plan showing who has influence at each stage, how decisions are recorded, what action follows and how power, consent and disagreement are handled.

relationships.note: Participants can help define a question that matters in their context.
Participation does not remove consent, privacy, safeguarding or power obligations.

limitations: Participation does not guarantee equal power, agreement or representativeness.
Action-oriented findings may be local and context-bound rather than generalisable to every community.
domain-item:participatory-and-action-res.meaning: Work with people affected by an issue so they can help shape the question, evidence, interpretation and possible action rather than being treated only as subjects.

domain-item:pilot-and-cognitive-pretesti.label: Piloting questions before fieldwork

requirement_scope.rationale: Cognitive pretesting is useful when developing questions or instruments; a pilot tests broader procedures. Neither is a generic requirement for work that does not design or administer an instrument.

domain-item:pilot-and-cognitive-pretesti.requirement_reason: A useful option for the work described above. It is not required for every Social Sciences student. You can continue without it and come back if you need it.
domain-item:pilot-and-cognitive-pretesti.learner_output: A pilot note listing confusing wording, practical problems and justified changes before the main study.

relationships.note: Piloting helps improve how ideas are measured.

limitations: This is especially relevant to surveys and structured instruments; it is not required for every project.
A pilot does not prove that the final study is unbiased.
domain-item:pilot-and-cognitive-pretesti.meaning: Try research questions or an instrument with a small group first to see whether people understand them as intended and whether the process works.

domain-item:programme-evaluation-and-the.label: Programme evaluation and theory of change

requirement_scope.rationale: Use when a programme, service or policy is assessed against intended outcomes, implementation, context or value; the decision question shapes the design.

domain-item:programme-evaluation-and-the.learner_output: An evaluation plan linking activities to outputs, outcomes and assumptions, with measures, context, evidence sources and decision limits.

relationships.note: The programme's purpose and evaluation questions determine what evidence is needed.
Causal designs are one possible part of an evaluation, not a requirement for every evaluation.

limitations: A theory of change makes assumptions visible; it does not prove that the programme caused the outcome.
Evaluation findings depend on context, measurement, implementation and the available comparison or baseline.
domain-item:programme-evaluation-and-the.meaning: Explain how a programme is expected to produce change, then gather evidence to judge its implementation, outcomes, value and limits.

domain-item:systematic-and-scoping-evide.label: Evidence synthesis: systematic reviews and scoping reviews

requirement_scope.condition: Find, screen, assess and combine existing studies rather than collecting new data by default.
requirement_scope.rationale: Use when a question is answered by systematically locating and synthesising existing evidence rather than collecting new primary data by default.

relationships.note: The review type, eligibility rules and search strategy must follow a focused question.
A traceable source library supports screening, deduplication, citation and an auditable review record.
A documented search, appraisal and synthesis makes the strength and limits of the evidence easier to explain.

limitations: Evidence synthesis is relevant to selected research, policy and practice tasks, not every this field role or project.
PRISMA is a reporting guideline, not a complete conduct method.
The Campbell course focuses on systematic reviews and meta-analysis and is advanced; it does not teach scoping review as a beginner pathway.
The JBI manual is formal method guidance, not an introductory course and is specifically grounded in JBI methods.
domain-item:systematic-and-scoping-evide.meaning: Evidence synthesis uses a documented method to find, select, assess and bring together existing studies. A systematic review answers a focused question using predefined methods. A scoping review maps what evidence or concepts exist and where evidence gaps may be. They are related but not interchangeable.

domain-method:network-analysis.label: Network analysis
domain-method:network-analysis.plain_language_meaning: A family of methods for representing entities as nodes and their relationships as edges, then examining the resulting structure or patterns.
domain-method:network-analysis.meaning_in_domain: In this field, network analysis is relevant when relationships among people, organisations, places or digital entities are central to the question. Social network analysis is the social-science-focused branch when the nodes and ties represent social actors and relations.
limitations: The analysis depends on how the network boundary and ties were defined and on whether relevant connections were observed.
Network patterns alone do not establish why ties formed or prove that network position caused an outcome.
domain-method:network-analysis.condition: Choose Network Analysis when the research question concerns the structure of connections among defined people, organisations or other entities.
domain-method:network-analysis.meaning: Network Analysis represents entities as points and their recorded connections as links, then examines patterns in those connections.
domain-method:network-analysis.learner_output: A documented network dataset and analysis that define the entities and links, report selected measures and explain coverage and interpretation limits.

domain-method:social-network-analysis.label: Social network analysis
domain-method:social-network-analysis.plain_language_meaning: A way to study relationships between people, groups or other social actors by defining who or what counts as a node and which connections count as ties, then analysing the resulting network.
domain-method:social-network-analysis.meaning_in_domain: In this field it is useful only when relationships themselves are part of the research question. It is not the same as analysing social-media content, and a graph picture alone does not establish a social finding.
limitations: The network boundary and tie definition determine what can be seen; incomplete or sensitive relationship data need careful handling.
A network measure does not by itself explain a person's behaviour, establish causation or represent people outside the observed network.
domain-method:social-network-analysis.condition: Choose Social Network Analysis when the question is specifically about social ties or relationship patterns among people, groups or organisations.
domain-method:social-network-analysis.meaning: Social Network Analysis studies how relationships among people or organisations are patterned and how those patterns relate to a social question.
domain-method:social-network-analysis.learner_output: A clearly bounded social network with documented actors and ties, a justified measure or comparison, and a plain-language interpretation that notes missing ties and uncertainty.

domain:D078.label: Social Sciences & Behavioural Research
domain:D078.overview: The social sciences study people, groups and societies: how people relate, how shared arrangements such as families, schools, workplaces and governments shape everyday life, and how societies change. A research question guides what evidence (information that can help answer it) researchers gather or examine and which research methods (planned ways to gather or examine information) they use. Researchers compare evidence with possible explanations and report what it supports, what remains uncertain and why.

overview_evidence.title: International Sociological Association, Social Distancing: The Relevance of Sociology

overview_evidence.supports: Student-friendly illustration of social relationships and group life; not a definition of every Social Sciences discipline.

student_orientation.whatItStudies: Sociology examines relationships, groups and social institutions (lasting arrangements and organizations that shape shared life). Economics studies how people make choices when resources are limited; political science studies public decisions and who can make them; behavioural research asks how people think and act, and how other people and settings influence behaviour. These fields can overlap, so the social question guides which perspectives help.
student_orientation.whatPeopleDo: Researchers ask questions, observe activity or examine documents, administrative records (information created when organizations register people or provide services, usually for purposes other than research) and digital traces (records created when people use digital services, such as posts, searches or purchases). They may count or measure information, interpret words or actions in their setting, or combine approaches. They check whose activity may be missing and protect private information.
questions: How do relationships in families and communities, workplaces and public organizations shape choices and opportunities?
How does access to money, services or decision-making power differ among groups, and how do people respond?
How do shared practices, organizations and societies change over time?
What evidence shows whether a public service or community programme reaches the people it was designed to support?
outputs: A question and study plan naming the people, places or records needed, how they will be gathered or examined, and what the study cannot establish.
Organized survey answers, interview accounts, observations, documents or service records, handled with appropriate care.
Tables, summaries or comparisons showing patterns and differences in the collected information.
A report explaining what the evidence supports, where it is uncertain and what a reader can reasonably conclude.
howWorkHappens: Start with a focused question about people, groups, shared arrangements or social change.

Choose evidence that fits: a survey uses planned questions to gather comparable answers; an interview is a guided conversation that gathers accounts; observation means watching and recording what happens; document research examines existing texts and records, including who created them, why and whose views may be missing.

When people take part, explain what the study asks them to do and how their information will be used. Seek informed consent (a voluntary decision made after receiving clear information) and follow the appropriate ethics review (a review of possible harm, participant rights, privacy and safeguards).
Compare the evidence with the question, consider other explanations and state what the study can support, what remains uncertain and what further evidence may be needed.
student_orientation.whereProgrammeFits: Your Sociology programme is one route into the wider social sciences. Its recorded course themes include social relationships, culture (shared ways of living and making meaning), family, inequality (unequal access to resources, opportunities or influence), crime, social change and research. These give context for the wider field. A course outcome is a learning goal recorded for a course; it describes programme content, not proof that a student has mastered it.

programme-theme:sociology:african_societ.label: African and Nigerian societies
programme-theme:sociology:african_societ.description: These courses examine African and Nigerian social structures, cultures, histories and regional settings.
programme-theme:sociology:african_societ.narration: You will study the histories, cultures, languages, institutions and social organisation of Nigerian and other African societies. Regional examples help you compare how societies differ and change. They are not presented as one story that describes every community.

programme-theme:sociology:applied_practi.label: Social work and practical change
programme-theme:sociology:applied_practi.description: These courses connect social-science knowledge with social work, community services, innovation and practical responses to social needs.
programme-theme:sociology:applied_practi.narration: You will consider social causes of problems and the services and organisations that respond to them, then explore how social-science knowledge can support practical ideas and services. The curriculum’s examples are learning topics, not a guarantee of professional qualification.

programme-theme:sociology:governance.label: Politics and organisations
programme-theme:sociology:governance.description: These courses examine political life, collective action, formal organisations and how institutions work with society.
programme-theme:sociology:governance.narration: You will study how social conditions influence political activity, parties and movements, and how formal organisations are structured and operate. This connects institutions to the people and communities around them.

programme-theme:sociology:ideas.label: Ideas and foundations
programme-theme:sociology:ideas.description: Courses in this part introduce the concepts, history and theories used to make sense of the programme’s subject area.
programme-theme:sociology:ideas.narration: You will learn how Sociology developed, explore key concepts and compare sociological theories. The programme uses these ideas to help explain social institutions, relationships and change.

programme-theme:sociology:people.label: People, groups and society
programme-theme:sociology:people.description: Courses in this part help you examine the people, groups, institutions, cultures or systems named in the programme record.
programme-theme:sociology:people.narration: You will examine how people behave and relate to one another, and how families, groups, culture, language and social settings shape everyday life. The courses draw on Sociology, Anthropology and Psychology while keeping their different viewpoints distinct.

programme-theme:sociology:research.label: Research and evidence
programme-theme:sociology:research.description: Courses in this part show how the programme asks questions, gathers information, examines evidence and communicates findings.
programme-theme:sociology:research.narration: You will move from forming a research question and planning a study to choosing suitable methods, collecting and analysing information, and explaining what the evidence can-and cannot-show. The curriculum includes quantitative approaches, which work with numbers, and qualitative approaches, which examine words, experiences and meaning.

programme-theme:sociology:shared_communi.label: Communication and academic writing
programme-theme:sociology:shared_communi.description: Shared university learning in clear English, reading, writing, reasoning and presenting ideas.
programme-theme:sociology:shared_communi.narration: You will practise communicating clearly in speech and writing, understanding written information, and presenting ideas. These are shared university skills that support your Sociology studies. The course does not replace the discipline-specific research and reporting taught elsewhere in the programme.

programme-theme:sociology:shared_enterpr.label: Entrepreneurship and venture creation
programme-theme:sociology:shared_enterpr.description: Shared courses on identifying opportunities, developing ideas and understanding how ventures are planned.
programme-theme:sociology:shared_enterpr.narration: You will explore how people identify an unmet need, develop an idea and plan a possible venture. These shared courses introduce entrepreneurship and venture creation. They do not promise that an idea will succeed or replace Sociology's study of social and economic conditions.

programme-theme:sociology:shared_nigeria.label: Nigerian peoples and culture
programme-theme:sociology:shared_nigeria.description: A shared course on Nigerian peoples, history, culture and social life.
programme-theme:sociology:shared_nigeria.narration: You will study Nigerian peoples and cultures through historical and social examples. This shared course adds Nigerian context to your university learning. It is not a complete account of every community or a substitute for the Sociology programme's own African and Nigerian society courses.

programme-theme:sociology:shared_peace_c.label: Peace, conflict and security
programme-theme:sociology:shared_peace_c.description: A shared course introducing peace, conflict, security and ways people respond to conflict.
programme-theme:sociology:shared_peace_c.narration: You will learn key ways people describe peace, conflict and security, and consider how conflict can arise and be addressed. This shared course introduces broad concepts. The Sociology courses examine particular social institutions, inequalities and settings in greater depth.

programme-theme:sociology:shared_philoso.label: Philosophy and reasoning
programme-theme:sociology:shared_philoso.description: A shared course on philosophical questions, logic and clear reasoning.
programme-theme:sociology:shared_philoso.narration: You will examine philosophical questions and practise logic-checking whether reasons support a conclusion. These are shared reasoning foundations, while sociological theory and evidence are developed in the Sociology courses.

programme-theme:sociology:social_change.label: Social change and development
programme-theme:sociology:social_change.description: These courses explore how societies change, what shapes development and how those changes affect people and institutions.
programme-theme:sociology:social_change.narration: You will compare explanations of social change and development, then consider how economic, political and historical conditions affect families, institutions and communities. The curriculum includes African and Nigerian contexts as well as wider theories.

programme-theme:sociology:social_issues.label: Inequality, gender and social problems
programme-theme:sociology:social_issues.description: These courses examine inequality, gender relations, crime and other social problems, including their causes and effects.
programme-theme:sociology:social_issues.narration: You will examine how inequality and gender relations shape people’s opportunities, and how crime and other social problems affect communities. The courses compare explanations and responses rather than treating any single cause or solution as universal.

programme-theme:sociology:technology.label: Technology and information
programme-theme:sociology:technology.description: Courses in this part cover the digital applications and information practices recorded for the programme.
programme-theme:sociology:technology.narration: You will practise using a computer and common applications to create, organise and present information. The curriculum names these as general computing skills. It does not make a particular software brand a Sociology requirement.

source_references.title: Social Sciences CCMAS 2023
source_references.locator: Sociology curriculum context: social structures, culture, family, inequality, crime, social change and research; course/outcome rows remain the source of programme-specific claims.
source_references.supports: Nigerian social-science curriculum context; not a claim that every school teaches every topic in the same way.
source_references.limits: National benchmark curriculum; institution-specific course delivery can differ.

source_references.title: Sociological Research, Introduction to Sociology 3e
source_references.supports: Sociological research begins with a question and a study plan; surveys, observation, interviews, experiments and existing sources answer different kinds of questions and carry different limits.
source_references.locator: Section 2.2: research design and examples of primary data collection and secondary analysis; method choice depends on the question and context.
source_references.limits: An introductory textbook, not a substitute for local curriculum or research ethics requirements.

source_references.title: What Is Sociology? Introduction to Sociology 3e
source_references.supports: Sociology studies groups and group interactions, societies and social interactions from close relationships to large social settings.
source_references.locator: Section 1.1 opening definition and discussion of society, social institutions and individual/group settings.
source_references.limits: An introductory textbook account; examples explain core scope but do not cover every sociological tradition or local curriculum.

source_references.title: Consent: Research Ethics Guidance
source_references.publisher: UK Research and Innovation, Economic and Social Research Council
source_references.supports: Informed consent requires enough accessible information for a voluntary decision; it includes what participation and data use involve, possible withdrawal, and limits to confidentiality where relevant.
source_references.locator: Sections 'What is freely given informed consent?', 'Giving information to participants', 'Consent', and voluntary participation/withdrawal guidance.
source_references.limits: UKRI/ESRC guidance; the applicable institution, local ethics process and law govern each study. Consent can require a justified alternative in some designs.

role-item:102:genomics-essential.label: genomics
role-item:102:genomics-essential.meaning: Genomics studies the genetic information contained across an organism's genome. In family-history work, genetic matches can suggest possible relationships, but they require consent, privacy safeguards, specialist interpretation, and documentary evidence; they are not a medical diagnosis.

role-item:102:genomics-essential.role_application: A cautious account compares genetic findings with documentary evidence and records consent, privacy safeguards, and uncertainty.
role-item:102:genomics-essential.why_it_matters: Genetic evidence can add one kind of clue to family-history research, but it cannot establish a relationship on its own.

layers: Sociology programme with all 14 evidence-traceable themes and 236 outcomes
Social Sciences domain overview and explicitly supported programme-to-domain transfer context
Methods of investigation/research follow the compulsory foundations; method selection then reveals only route-linked Layer 2/3 preparation with conditions intact
Layer 2 field-wide knowledge and Layer 3 research practices are conditionally revealed after the learner chooses a method or exact named design
one or more selected methods; explain multi-select and require an exact named design for multi-method downstream
the selected method or exact named design filters which Layer 2/3 items appear below the method selector; do not union a combination's independent method inventories or duplicate records downstream
routing_policy.area_selection: Rank all seven canonical areas by task-family links from selected methods; do not hide non-top-ranked areas or infer that method choice alone establishes fit.
routing_policy.role_selection: Show roles only through their reviewed area links. Within a chosen area, rank by explicit role-task/item evidence when available; do not claim that the domain method is a role requirement merely because the role belongs to that area.
routing_policy.requirements: The three compulsory D078 domain foundations gate method choice. Other domain, area and role items keep their existing needed/useful/optional/conditional lane and remain non-blocking unless an approved route-scoped dependency explicitly says otherwise.
routing_policy.multiple_methods: Do not union independently selected method routes. Match the complete selected method set to an exact named design; when multiple designs match, require a design choice. Partial larger designs and unsupported sets have no combined downstream. Preserve asymmetric method contributions inside the selected design.
routing_policy.downstream_items: After method/combination selection, expose its task-linked area items, tool options, extensions and role items. The set is an available contextual branch; lane and task condition still determine whether each is needed, useful or optional.
routing_policy.relationship_edges: Only reviewed typed relationships with exact canonical targets and relationship-specific evidence are selectable. Prose alternatives remain item explanations unless a separately approved edge identifies the exact target and route.
